keyElements.director: Allison Anders, Alexandre Rockwell, Robert Rodriguez, Quentin Tarantino

sections.text: Four Rooms follows Ted the bellhop (Tim Roth) during his first night working at the surreal Mon Signor Hotel on New Year's Eve. Through four separate vignettes directed by different filmmakers, Ted encounters increasingly bizarre situations in different rooms. Roth's physical comedy performance channels silent film legends like Buster Keaton, though his manic energy sometimes feels overwrought. The anthology format allows each director to explore their signature styles, but the quality varies dramatically between segments.

Tim Roth's exaggerated performance serves as the connecting thread, though his character's quirks become repetitive across segments. The standout chapters come from Rodriguez and Tarantino, who inject their signature blend of dark humor and tension. Rodriguez's 'The Misbehavers' featuring Antonio Banderas shows the most consistent tone, while Tarantino's finale 'The Man from Hollywood' delivers sharp dialogue and mounting tension reminiscent of Reservoir Dogs (1992).

Released during the indie film boom of the 1990s, Four Rooms attempted to capitalize on the anthology format popularized by films like Tales from the Crypt (1989) and New York Stories (1989). The film represents the era's experimentation with narrative structure and the rising prominence of independent filmmakers, though it ultimately demonstrates the challenges of maintaining consistency across multiple directors.

The film's anthology structure draws from classics like Dead of Night (1945) while attempting to modernize the format with edgy 90s sensibilities. Each segment tackles different genres - from farce to crime thriller - though the transitions often feel jarring rather than complementary. The experiment paved the way for later anthology films like Sin City (2005) and Grindhouse (2007), which learned from Four Rooms' structural mistakes.

While uneven, Four Rooms remains an interesting snapshot of 90s independent cinema and the creative freedom filmmakers enjoyed during that era. Its influence can be seen in modern anthology series like The Ballad of Buster Scruggs (2018), though these later works demonstrate more cohesive vision and quality control. The film serves better as a curiosity for fans of the directors than as a standalone entertainment.
